pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Count backwards through zero into negative numbers (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2…), understand that negatives are less than zero, place them on a number line, and read them in context (temperature). The number line EXTENDS left past zero — the first genuinely new territory beyond the counting numbers.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): formal integers are Grade 6 (6.NS.5-6), but temperature/number-line intuition is built earlier; treat this as pre-integer number-line reasoning.
• Operational details — Build negatives on a horizontal or (temperature-style) vertical number line, counting continuously down through zero so the sequence's symmetry about 0 is felt. Anchor to a real context — the thermometer is ideal — so 'below zero' has meaning. Stress that −2 is less than −1 (further from zero going left = smaller), which contradicts children's 'bigger digit = bigger' intuition. Avoid formal negative arithmetic here; focus on ordering, counting, and reading in context.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): counts back through zero to −5 with a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): places negatives on a line and reads temperatures below zero. Tier C (age 9, extending): orders negatives correctly (−5 < −2) and explains why, using the line.
bestPractices: Count continuously DOWN through zero on a number line so the symmetry about 0 is experienced, not stated.
Anchor to the thermometer / temperature context — the most intuitive real model of below-zero.
Explicitly confront the 'bigger digit = bigger' clash: −5 is LESS than −2 because it is further left/colder.
Use a vertical number line (thermometer) as well as horizontal so direction-of-decrease is felt two ways.
Keep to counting/ordering/reading in context; defer negative arithmetic (adding/subtracting integers) to later.
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line extended left of zero
Number track counting down through zero
Real contexts: temperature, sea level, later bank balance/floors
commonMisconceptions: Believing zero is the smallest number, so negatives 'can't exist' or are 'just zero'.
Reading −3 as 'three' and losing the sign's meaning.
Miscounting across zero (skipping 0, or 1, 0, 1 back up).
Treating the minus as subtraction rather than a position/label below zero.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: counting backwards through zero into negative numbers, placing negatives on a number line, and reading them in context (temperature). The core insight is that the number line extends left past zero, and that −5 is LESS than −2 because it lies further from zero on the negative side — directly confronting the 'bigger digit = bigger' intuition. Work stays with counting, ordering, and reading in context; formal negative arithmetic is deferred. The primary vehicle is a number-line/thermometer activity the child drives, with reference images and conversational context as supports.

activities.title: Count down through zero on a thermometer line
feedback: If the child reverses upward at zero (0 then 1 again), extend the line/thermometer visibly below zero and re-count −1, −2, −3 so the continuation is seen; do not accept 'nothing is below zero'.
If the child says numbers stop at zero, anchor in a real below-zero context (temperature, floors below ground) so numbers less than zero are legitimate.
If the child reads −3 as 'three', pause and have them say 'negative three / three below zero' so the minus is read as a position/label below zero, not as a subtraction to carry out.
activities.rationale: Counting continuously down through zero lets the unbroken continuation past zero be experienced rather than merely stated, and the thermometer gives 'below zero' a concrete meaning. A horizontal line offers a second felt direction of decrease. A live, learner-driven scale (dragging the marker so the reading updates past zero) can make the continuation vivid, though a reference image or spoken counting can also support this.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Start at a reading (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical thermometer (or a horizontal number line) and count the marker down continuously: 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3, watching it pass zero in one unbroken descent rather than stopping or bouncing.
Narrate each step aloud, including the names of the negatives as the marker crosses zero.
Repeat the descent on a horizontal number line, moving steadily left through zero, to feel that the decrease keeps going in the same direction past zero (toggle between the two if available).
Then count back UP through zero from a negative start (e.g. −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1) to check the sequence works both ways.
activities.intendedInsight: Below-zero numbers are a genuine continuation of the counting sequence, not a separate set; the line extends left/below zero, and counting down keeps going in the same direction past zero. Only the number names repeat as mirror images (1 and −1, 2 and −2), and each step down still gives a smaller number.

activities.title: Order negatives: colder is lower is smaller
feedback: If the child ranks −5 as larger because 5 > 2, walk both onto a horizontal number line: −5 sits further left, and further left means smaller, so −5 < −2 even though 5 > 2.
Reinforce with the thermometer image: a lower reading is colder, and colder is a smaller temperature.
If the child names 0 as the smallest possible number, use a below-zero context so numbers less than zero are accepted as comparable.
activities.rationale: The −5 vs −2 comparison is the central misconception, so it deserves dedicated ordering practice with an explanation, not just the correct label. Tying 'smaller' to position (further left / further below zero / colder) gives the child a stable rule that survives the digit-size clash. A drag-to-order interaction where −5 correctly lands below −2 with 'colder = lower = smaller' feedback can make the mechanism concrete; ordering on paper with stated reasons works too.
sourceClaims: The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Given numbers such as −5, −2, 0, 3, place each on the scale and arrange them smallest to largest.
Specifically compare −2 and −5: place both and decide which is smaller, stating a reason.
Explain in words why −5 is smaller than −2 even though 5 is bigger than 2 — e.g. 'it is further below zero / further left / colder'.
Answer context questions: Is −10°C warmer or colder than −2°C? Which is bigger, −1 or 0?
activities.intendedInsight: On the negative side, further from zero (further left / lower / colder) means SMALLER, so −5 < −2, reversing the digit-size intuition.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: drop below zero
feedback: A child expecting numbers to stop predicts 0 or 'it can't go lower'; show the continuation below zero and re-count through zero to −2.
A child who predicts −2 and justifies by continuing past zero (…1, 0, −1, −2) has the target understanding; ask them to explain the crossing point.
Follow-up probes: What comes after −3 if I keep counting back? If I started at −4 and counted up through zero, what would I say?
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task surfaces the 'numbers stop at zero' and magnitude-ordering misconceptions through the child's stated reason before the answer is revealed, making the diagnostic value come from the justification rather than the final label.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
learnerActions: Set a thermometer to 3°C. Before moving anything, predict the reading after it drops 5 degrees, and say WHY.
Commit to the prediction and reason out loud (the reasoning is the important part).
Then slide/count the marker down 5 steps through zero to check against the prediction.
Discuss any mismatch: where did the count cross zero, and what came after?
activities.intendedInsight: Counting down past zero from 3 by 5 reaches −2 (3 − 5 = −2); numbers do not stop at zero, and predicting forces the child to apply the continuation rather than read it off.

activities.title: Negatives in the real world (context talk)
feedback: If the child treats −20 as warmer than −5 because 20 > 5, return to the thermometer: −20 is lower, so colder and smaller.
Keep the focus on ordering and reading; do not drift into adding/subtracting negatives.
activities.rationale: Context motivates and reinforces, and reading real sub-zero values gives extra ordering practice; the ordering rule itself is secured on the line, so context work supports and applies the idea rather than being the only route to it.
learnerActions: Discuss or read about places and situations with below-zero values: last night's temperatures, a polar region at −20°C vs −5°C, sea level, floors below ground.
Decide which of two sub-zero values is colder/lower and justify using the line idea.
Match a few real readings (e.g. fridge, freezer, a frosty morning) to positions on a thermometer scale.
activities.intendedInsight: Negative numbers describe real quantities below a chosen zero, giving the abstract line a meaningful anchor and extra ordering practice.

constraints: Keep to counting, ordering, and reading negatives in context; defer formal negative arithmetic (adding/subtracting integers) to later.
Explicitly confront the 'bigger digit = bigger' clash: −5 is less than −2 because it is further left / lower / colder.

A static thermometer or number-line poster is a useful reference and can support counting, but cannot itself be dragged or stepped; pair it with active ordering/counting on a line rather than relying on it alone.
Conversation/context framing (e.g. a polar scientist) can motivate and give extra ordering practice, but should not be the sole route to the ordering concept.
US note: formal integers are Grade 6 (CCSS-M 6.NS.5-6); for this age treat the work as pre-integer number-line and temperature intuition.
When counting across zero, guard against skipping 0 or bouncing (1, 0, 1); ensure zero is named as a step and the sequence continues below it.
reviewNotes: Independent editorial review performed on the saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched and no fresh source verification, human review, or empirical effectiveness testing occurred. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of three cited sources (CCSS-M Grade 6; NCETM guidance) were marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE Year 4 claim was marked verified:true. Evidence strength is unchanged and not independently confirmed here.

The CCSS-M Grade 6 claim is retained only as standards-placement context (US constraint); it is correctly not used as a sourceClaim for the context activity, because it does not establish that activity's teaching principle (context supports while ordering is secured on the line).

The original noted 3D 'adds nothing'. That is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; a 3D treatment is simply not needed because the concept is essentially one-dimensional (a line/scale). Softened accordingly.
Arithmetic check: starting at 3°C and dropping 5 degrees gives −2°C (3 − 5 = −2); matches the source and the predict-then-check activity.
Ordering checks: −5 < −2 is correct (further from zero on the negative side is smaller); −10°C and −20°C are colder/smaller than −2°C and −5°C respectively.

The 'minus read as subtraction' misconception from the source is covered only indirectly via the sign-meaning feedback in the first activity; it could warrant a more explicit treatment if expanded later.

assess.poeTask: Set a model thermometer to 3°C. Before moving anything, ask the child to predict the reading after it drops 5 degrees and to say why. A child who thinks numbers stop at zero predicts 0 (or 'it can't go lower'); a child who understands negatives predicts −2. Then slide the marker down through zero to check — the pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I keep counting back, what comes after −3?
On a thermometer, is −10°C warmer or colder than −2°C — why?
Which is bigger, −1 or 0? How can you tell?
What if I started at −4 and counted UP through zero — what would I say?
assess.correctAnswer: After 0 comes −1, −2, −3 … −5 is smaller than −2 because it is further below zero (further left on the number line).

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude — '−5 is bigger than −2 because 5 is bigger than 2'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk both on a horizontal number line; show −5 sits further left, and 'smaller' means further left, so −5 < −2 even though 5 > 2.
errorPatterns.distractor: −2 is smaller, because 2 is less than 5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks −5 as the larger / −2 as the smaller, reasoning from the digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Numbers stop at (or bounce off) zero — after 0 the child says 1 again, treating zero as the floor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the number line and a thermometer below zero so the sequence −1, −2, −3 is seen as a real continuation; do not accept 'nothing is below zero'.
errorPatterns.distractor: After 0 you go back up to 1.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counting back reaches 0 and then reverses upward, or child says 'you can't go past zero'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Zero-as-smallest — believes 0 is the least possible number, so there is no answer 'below' it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a context that clearly goes below zero (temperature, floors below ground) to establish numbers less than zero as legitimate.
errorPatterns.distractor: Zero — it's the smallest, nothing is less.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names 0 as the smallest number when asked, or refuses to compare negatives.

responseLevels.gap: Stops or bounces at zero, or orders negatives purely by digit size.
responseLevels.full: Continues the sequence past zero and orders negatives by position on the number line, justifying that further-left / further-below-zero means smaller, and applies it in context (temperature).
responseLevels.partial: Counts back through zero correctly but reverts to magnitude reasoning when comparing two negatives (−5 vs −2).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count back from 3, out loud: 3, 2, 1, 0 ... what comes next? And which is smaller, −2 or −5? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the number line continues past zero into negatives and knows −5 is smaller because it is further from zero the other way. A child treating negatives as ordinary numbers picks −2 as smaller (2<5), and a child who thinks numbers stop at zero bounces back to 1. The justification, not the label, reveals which.
